paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet allocation, or LDA, is a probabilistic model used in applications including document analysis and computer vision. Using it requires inference: estimating the hidden structure that could explain observed data. This paper addresses the computational difficulty of that step when applications involve large amounts of data.

The authors propose a collapsed variational Bayesian inference algorithm for LDA. Their contribution concerns how to perform inference within the model, rather than replacing LDA with a different model. The motivation is that existing approaches, including standard variational Bayes and Gibbs sampling, have proved inadequate for the large scale applications the authors discuss.

The paper reports that the proposed algorithm is computationally efficient, straightforward to implement, and significantly more accurate than standard variational Bayesian inference for LDA. These findings connect practical usability with inference quality: an approximation is more useful if it can handle substantial workloads while preserving accuracy. The explicit accuracy comparison is with standard variational Bayes; the abstract does not claim an accuracy advantage over Gibbs sampling.
neurips-2006-a-collapsed-variational-bay.tldr: A collapsed variational inference algorithm makes LDA inference efficient and easy to implement while improving accuracy over standard variational Bayes.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to evaluate Go positions by learning from recorded games. The central challenge is connecting small tactical patterns to an assessment of the whole board. A useful evaluation method must accommodate a growing collection of patterns, interactions between different regions, and changes in board size.

The system learns the propensities of local patterns from a game library. It feeds these values and other tactical information into a recursive neural network whose architecture comes from a Bayesian network. The network combines information across the board and predicts the probability that each local region belongs to either player. Combining those probabilities gives an estimate of expected territory at the end of the game or another stage.

Human games provide the local territory targets needed for training. The authors report that a system trained only on amateur games played on a 9-by-9 board performs surprisingly well on a test set drawn from professional 19-by-19 games. That finding supports the approach's ability to transfer across board sizes and game sources in the reported evaluation.
neurips-2006-a-scalable-machine-learning.tldr: A recursive neural network combines learned local Go patterns into territory estimates that transfer well from small amateur boards to a larger professional-game test set.

paragraphs: This paper studies how networks form when participants choose which connections to buy. Each player balances spending on edges against the average network distance to everyone else. The model connects individual economic decisions with a global question: when will the resulting network keep even its most distant participants close together?

The authors establish a sharp threshold for equilibrium networks in two dimensions. Below the threshold value of two for the model's distance-cost parameter, every Nash equilibrium has a diameter bounded independently of network size. Above two, every equilibrium has a diameter that grows as a root of network size. The supplied abstract has missing mathematical symbols, so it does not fully specify the cost formula.

The distinction is between networks whose maximum separation stays bounded as they expand and networks whose maximum separation keeps increasing. The theoretical results extend to higher dimensions. The authors also compare their findings with an earlier stochastic model and empirically examine navigability, asking how equilibrium network structure relates to the ability to find routes.
neurips-2006-a-small-world-threshold-for.tldr: A network formation game exhibits a threshold separating equilibria with size-independent diameter from equilibria whose diameter grows with network size.

paragraphs: Given two stereo images, this paper jointly estimates pixel disparities and a scene's division into foreground and background. Disparity describes the displacement between corresponding image locations. The challenge is to represent regions that vary smoothly while also preserving abrupt changes associated with scene boundaries and occlusion.

The authors use a Gaussian process whose covariance depends on segmentation labels for foreground, background, and occlusion. These labels change how the model represents relationships between image locations, giving the method its name: a switched Gaussian process. Connecting segmentation with covariance lets a single probabilistic framework accommodate both smooth regions and discontinuities.

A greedy incremental algorithm adds observations and assigns segmentation labels. The authors describe two ways to choose observations: processing scanlines independently, or using an active learning criterion to select a sparse set of points to measure. They report performance comparable to leading methods. The contribution is therefore a joint probabilistic treatment of disparity and segmentation, together with alternative schedules for gathering the observations used in inference.
neurips-2006-a-switched-gaussian-process.tldr: A Gaussian process controlled by segmentation labels jointly estimates stereo disparity and scene layers while representing both smooth regions and discontinuities.

paragraphs: This paper introduces adaptor grammars as a way to describe probabilistic language models. They extend probabilistic context-free grammars, which express language structure through rules with probabilities. The extension allows successive uses of grammatical rules to be dependent, expanding the kinds of statistical relationships that a grammar can represent.

The added components, called adaptors, supply those dependencies. With an adaptor based on the Pitman-Yor process, the framework can express nonparametric Bayesian language models involving Dirichlet processes and hierarchical Dirichlet processes as simple grammars. This connects a grammatical description of language with models usually described through more specialized probabilistic constructions.

The authors also provide a general inference algorithm for adaptor grammars and show how several existing models fit into the framework. The practical value is that defining a model and carrying out inference become parts of a shared approach. Researchers can specify a language model through grammar structure while using a general computational method, rather than treating every supported probabilistic construction as a separate modeling system.
neurips-2006-adaptor-grammars-a-framewor.tldr: Adaptor grammars extend probabilistic grammars with dependencies between uses, providing a common language and inference algorithm for several nonparametric Bayesian models.

paragraphs: Planning becomes difficult when an agent cannot fully observe its environment. Breaking a task into smaller planning problems can help, but many approaches require someone to supply that hierarchy in advance. This paper investigates how to discover the hierarchy automatically while optimizing the policy that uses it.

The authors formulate hierarchical policy optimization as a non-convex optimization problem. The hierarchy itself is represented by variables, allowing its structure to be chosen during optimization. They describe approaches using general nonlinear solvers, a mixed-integer nonlinear approximation, and bounded hierarchical policy iteration. Known pieces of the hierarchy can be fixed from prior knowledge while the remaining pieces are learned.

The framework can discover hierarchical policies that include recursion. The authors state that such policies can be more compact, potentially requiring infinitely fewer parameters, and are often easier to understand through their decomposition. The significance is that task organization becomes part of the planning problem rather than a prerequisite supplied entirely by a designer. Compactness and interpretability are possible benefits of the discovered structure.
neurips-2006-automated-hierarchy-discove.tldr: Encoding policy hierarchy as optimization variables lets a planner discover task decompositions, including recursive structures, in partially observable environments.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a reinforcement learning policy by estimating how changes to its parameters affect performance. Conventional methods use Monte Carlo sampling to estimate that direction of improvement. Because these estimates tend to have high variance, obtaining a sufficiently accurate direction can require many samples and slow learning.

This paper proposes a Bayesian framework that models the policy gradient as a Gaussian process. The aim is to use the available observations more effectively when estimating how the policy should change. The authors report that the framework reduces the number of samples required to obtain accurate gradient estimates, directly addressing the sampling burden of conventional methods.

The framework also supplies estimates of the natural gradient and quantifies uncertainty in its gradient estimates at little additional cost. Thus, its output includes both an improvement direction and information about how uncertain that direction is. The contribution combines greater sample efficiency in gradient estimation with additional information useful for understanding the reliability of a policy update.
neurips-2006-bayesian-policy-gradient-al.tldr: A Gaussian-process model of policy gradients reduces the samples needed for accurate estimates and provides natural gradients and uncertainty at little extra cost.

paragraphs: This paper addresses gene prediction by combining comparative sequence information with additional evidence. The authors argue that further progress requires incorporating more kinds of data than established generative models readily accommodate. Their approach uses a conditional random field to predict hidden gene-related states directly from observed information.

The implemented model includes a phylogenetic generalized hidden Markov model as its comparative baseline and adds non-probabilistic features. A conditional random field provides a common framework for these different forms of evidence. This makes the modeling contribution concrete: retain the comparative sequence model while allowing additional signals to contribute through discriminative training.

The authors test the approach on the genome of Cryptococcus neoformans, a fungal human pathogen. Their baseline achieves accuracy comparable to the best available gene prediction tool for that organism, and they report significant improvements from discriminative training and added non-probabilistic evidence. The findings support combining these sources of information in the tested setting. The resulting software, Conrad, is described as freely available under an open source license.
neurips-2006-comparative-gene-prediction.tldr: A conditional random field combines comparative sequence modeling with additional evidence and significantly improves gene prediction in the tested fungal genome.

paragraphs: Geometric dimensionality reduction tries to describe data through the shape of an underlying manifold. In practice, an algorithm receives a cloud of sampled points rather than the continuous manifold itself. This paper addresses the theoretical connection between a spectral construction on those points and the geometry it is intended to represent.

The authors prove convergence of the point cloud Laplacian's eigenvectors to eigenfunctions of the manifold's Laplace-Beltrami operator. These are the discrete and continuous objects on the two sides of the result. In plain language, the theorem connects patterns computed from sampled data with corresponding patterns defined on the underlying geometric surface.

That connection gives theoretical support to Laplacian Eigenmaps as a spectral dimensionality reduction method in the manifold setting. The abstract identifies the result as the first convergence result for such an algorithm in that setting. Its contribution is a mathematical foundation: the quantities used by the discrete method converge to meaningful continuous counterparts, linking a data-based representation to the geometry of the space being sampled.
neurips-2006-convergence-of-laplacian-ei.tldr: The paper proves that point cloud Laplacian eigenvectors converge to their continuous manifold counterparts, establishing a foundation for Laplacian Eigenmaps.

paragraphs: A spam filter may learn from labeled public messages even though an individual user's inbox contains a different mix of email. This paper treats that mismatch as a central learning problem. The target is performance on each user's own unknown message distribution, for which only unlabeled inbox messages are available.

The authors develop a method that minimizes loss with respect to the user's personal distribution using the biased labeled sample. They also introduce a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian model that shares information across users. It learns a common prior that can be applied to new accounts, combining personalization with knowledge gathered from other users.

The reported empirical results support both parts of the approach. Correcting sample bias outperforms learning that naively treats the available data as identically distributed. Sharing information through the Dirichlet-based model outperforms both one common filter and independently trained user filters. Together, these findings suggest that adapting to each inbox and pooling information across inboxes can work productively in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2006-dirichlet-enhanced-spam-fil.tldr: Correcting training-sample bias and sharing Bayesian information across users improves personalized spam filtering in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper separates changing foreground objects from changing backgrounds in image collections and video. It first divides images into segments, turning a decision for every pixel into a supervised foreground-or-background decision for each segment. That reduces the dimensionality of the labeling problem while allowing decisions to use appearance information from within a region.

The method samples random patches adaptively inside each segment and maintains two collections of examples, one for foreground and one for background. New patches undergo a bidirectional consistency check against these collections. This check rejects outliers and controls how readily the appearance models adapt. Partitioning and resampling patches further updates the models as new observations arrive.

To label a segment, the system combines patch similarities to the two appearance models into a final decision. The authors validate the approach through real examples of object-level image mapping and tracking in challenging environments, including non-rigid objects in surveillance videos. The approach's value lies in pairing a simple segment-level decision with appearance models that evolve as the scene changes.
neurips-2006-dynamic-foreground-backgrou.tldr: Adaptive collections of random image patches support segment-level foreground extraction and tracking as object and background appearances change.

paragraphs: Deep networks can represent some functions much more compactly than shallow architectures, but finding good parameters is a separate challenge. This paper examines the observation that gradient-based training from random initialization often appears to reach poor solutions. It studies a greedy, layer-by-layer unsupervised training strategy introduced for deep belief networks.

The authors investigate the strategy empirically and explore variants. They consider continuous inputs and supervised tasks where the structure of the input distribution does not sufficiently reveal what needs to be predicted. These extensions address an important distinction: learning useful structure in inputs and learning what matters for a prediction task are not automatically the same objective.

The experiments support the hypothesis that unsupervised layer-wise training mainly helps optimization by placing the weights near a good local minimum. The resulting internal distributed representations capture higher-level abstractions of the input and lead to better generalization in the experiments. The finding offers an explanation for the strategy's success: preparing the network's layers can make subsequent optimization start from a more promising region.
neurips-2006-greedy-layer-wise-training-.tldr: Experiments support the view that greedy unsupervised layer-wise training improves deep networks mainly by providing a better starting point for optimization.

paragraphs: A search engine earning money from clicks must choose between displaying ads known to appeal to users and testing new ads whose appeal is uncertain. Testing can reveal valuable information, but it takes display opportunities away from established ads. This paper studies that exploration-versus-exploitation tradeoff with revenue as the objective.

The authors model advertisement placement as a multi-armed bandit problem. They extend traditional bandit formulations to incorporate advertiser budget constraints. The motivation also includes finite advertisement lifetimes: both budgets and limited availability make it necessary to consider learning about new ads alongside earning revenue from currently promising ones.

The paper derives theoretical performance bounds for a family of algorithms and evaluates empirical performance through extensive experiments on real-world data. These contributions address two complementary questions: what guarantees can be established within the model, and how the algorithms behave on observed advertising data. The supplied abstract reports the evaluation without specifying a winning algorithm or numerical gains. The main contribution is bringing market constraints into the sequential decision problem.
neurips-2006-handling-advertisements-of-.tldr: The paper models search-ad selection as a budget-constrained bandit problem and develops performance bounds and empirical evaluations for algorithms balancing exploration and revenue.

paragraphs: This paper studies policy evaluation in reinforcement learning with a linear function approximator. Least-squares temporal difference learning, or LSTD, is data efficient, but its computational cost grows quadratically with the number of parameters. Incremental LSTD aims to obtain similar results with a cost that grows linearly, making larger representations more practical.

The authors generalize the existing incremental algorithm and provide its first convergence proof for an iLSTD algorithm. They also extend it to include eligibility traces, which allow learning updates to incorporate information associated with earlier experience. The extension preserves the algorithm's asymptotic computational complexity, so this added capability does not change its stated linear scaling.

The empirical study uses mountain car with 10,000 features, a representation large enough to demonstrate substantial computational advantages over LSTD. The contribution combines theoretical support, an expanded learning mechanism, and evidence at a scale where the computational distinction matters. The convergence result applies to an iLSTD algorithm as established in the paper, while the reported practical advantage is demonstrated on the specified evaluation problem.
neurips-2006-ilstd-eligibility-traces-an.tldr: The paper adds a convergence proof and eligibility traces to iLSTD while retaining linear computational scaling and demonstrating advantages with 10,000 features.

paragraphs: Microelectrode arrays used in cortical prostheses record many neural signals at once. Processing these high-dimensional recordings is challenging, especially when different electrodes carry overlapping information. This paper proposes an analog-to-digital conversion architecture that performs conversion and spatial decorrelation together, addressing redundancy at the point where signals become digital.

The architecture has multiple inputs and outputs and is based on min-max gradient descent applied to a regularized linear cost function. An online formulation allows it to adapt to slow changes in correlations between channels. Such changes can arise when microelectrodes move relative to the sources of the recorded signals.

Experiments with real multichannel neural recordings demonstrate reduced redundancy across electrodes and compression performed directly at the converter. The significance is the integration of two operations within one module: digitizing the measurements and reducing information repeated across channels. The stated adaptive capability concerns slow correlation changes, connecting the method to the changing relationship between electrode positions and signal sources described by the authors.
neurips-2006-large-margin-multi-channel-.tldr: A multichannel converter combines digitization with adaptive decorrelation to reduce redundancy and compress recorded neural signals directly during conversion.

paragraphs: Objects can often be organized into a hierarchy of categories, but a hierarchy alone does not explain which categories matter for particular observations. This paper learns annotated hierarchies from object features and relationships. Its goal is to identify both a category structure and the categories most useful for describing each feature or relation.

In the proposed representation, internal nodes identify categories of objects. Annotations connect those categories to the observed properties and relationships they help describe. The authors define a generative model for the hierarchy, its annotations, and the associated data. They then develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo method to learn the structure.

The model discovers interpretable organization in several real-world datasets. The meaning of that result goes beyond grouping similar objects: the learned annotations also explain how the grouping relates to individual features and relations. This makes the hierarchy a structured description of the data, with category membership and the usefulness of different categories learned within the same probabilistic framework.
neurips-2006-learning-annotated-hierarch.tldr: A generative model learns object hierarchies annotated with the categories that best describe particular features and relationships.

paragraphs: Transductive regression predicts values for test points that are already visible to the learning algorithm, although their labels are unknown. This paper studies how to use that information when unlabeled data greatly outnumber labeled examples. Knowing the test inputs creates an opportunity to make their locations part of the learning process.

The authors derive explicit error bounds based on VC dimension for all bounded loss functions. When applied to classification, the bounds coincide with Vapnik's tight classification bounds. They also develop a regression algorithm inspired by the analysis. It first uses the locations of unlabeled points to estimate labels locally, then applies a global optimization to produce robust predictions.

The algorithm has closed-form solutions in both primal and kernelized forms and is designed to handle large quantities of unlabeled data efficiently. Experiments on public regression datasets include up to 20,000 unlabeled examples. Comparisons with other transductive regression methods show good performance and scalability in those evaluations, connecting the theoretical analysis to a computationally practical prediction method.
neurips-2006-on-transductive-regression-.tldr: The paper develops error bounds and a scalable transductive regression algorithm that combines local label estimates with global optimization.

paragraphs: Detecting a real change in sensory input requires balancing speed against the risk of reacting to noise. This paper formalizes an instance of that problem using tools from controlled stochastic processes. Under certain assumptions, the authors characterize the Bayesian decision policy that optimally balances the competing demands.

From that policy, they derive a process for accumulating information and deciding when a change has occurred. Its dynamics closely resemble those of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron. This correspondence supplies a computational interpretation of neuronal properties, including resting membrane potential, voltage-dependent conductance, and the voltage to which a neuron resets after a spike.

The authors also examine how timing, uncertainty, neuromodulation, and reward affect the optimal strategy and neuronal sensitivity. The resemblance between the derived decision process and a spiking neuron suggests that neurons may be optimized for tracking changes in their inputs. This is an interpretation supported by the modeled correspondence under the paper's assumptions, rather than a universal demonstration that every neuron implements an optimal detector.
neurips-2006-optimal-change-detection-an.tldr: Under specified assumptions, optimal Bayesian change detection yields dynamics resembling a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron.

paragraphs: Matching two shapes becomes difficult when their parts vary independently. This paper proposes a probabilistic method that learns the parts while finding correspondences between shapes. Each part receives its own transformation, allowing the match to account for variation at the part level rather than treating the shape as one inseparable object.

Shapes are represented as unlabeled point sets of arbitrary size. Ideas from semi-supervised learning bias the discovered parts toward perceptually meaningful structures. A background component accommodates occlusion, local differences, and clutter, so observations that do not fit the shared part structure can be handled within the model. This supports application to shapes extracted from real images.

An expectation-maximization algorithm alternates between estimating soft correspondences and optimizing the transformations of individual parts through Procrustes analysis. Soft correspondence represents uncertainty about which points should match. Alternating the two steps couples the correspondence problem with the search for appropriate part transformations. The central contribution is that matching and discovering the shape's parts are solved together within a probabilistic framework.
neurips-2006-part-based-probabilistic-po.tldr: A probabilistic matching method jointly learns shape parts, their independent transformations, and uncertain point correspondences while accommodating clutter and occlusion.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the problem of recovering two people's speech from a single recording in which their voices are mixed. The system uses models of how speech evolves over time to infer the individual source signals. Temporal structure supplies information for deciding which portions of the mixed sound belong to each talker.

After estimating the separate speech signals, the system passes them to a conventional speech recognizer. This separates the inference of source speech from the subsequent recognition step. The authors report performance on par with human listeners for the two-talker task, with recognition exceeding human performance under many of the evaluated conditions.

The system achieves its best results when its model of temporal dynamics closely reflects the task's grammatical constraints. This finding identifies the fit between the model and the speech task as an important part of the reported success. The contribution is evidence that suitable temporal models can support strong separation and recognition from one channel, with the strongest performance tied to accurately capturing the task's allowed speech structure.
neurips-2006-single-channel-speech-separ.tldr: Temporal speech models enable human-comparable two-talker separation, with the best performance when their dynamics closely match the task's grammatical constraints.

paragraphs: This paper develops a feature extraction method for labeled data using a new kernel orthonormalized partial least squares variant. Feature extraction seeks a representation that retains useful information in fewer variables. The authors focus on obtaining expressive features while making the method suitable for larger datasets.

Their approach imposes sparsity constraints on the solution to improve scalability. This brings the complexity of the learned representation into the design of the method itself. The intended combination is a kernel-based model with strong expressive capacity and a sparse solution that makes feature extraction more manageable as the amount of data grows.

The algorithm is evaluated on a benchmark of UCI datasets and on music genre prediction using integrated short-time music features. The authors report strong expressive power with relatively few extracted features and clear improvements over ordinary kernel PLS in their evaluations. These results support the method as an option for supervised feature extraction, particularly when a compact representation must still preserve information useful for the prediction task.
neurips-2006-sparse-kernel-orthonormaliz.tldr: A sparse kernel orthonormalized PLS method produces expressive compact features and outperforms ordinary kernel PLS in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Clustering stability asks whether changing the observed data changes the resulting groups. This paper studies that question for K-means by expressing it as empirical risk minimization over a class of functions. The authors explicitly calculate the class's covering number and connect stability to its geometry relative to the underlying data distribution.

The analysis distinguishes a unique global minimizer from multiple global minimizers. With a unique minimizer, the clustering solution is stable even under complete changes of the data in the setting analyzed. With multiple minimizers, changing a number of samples on the order of the square root of the sample size marks the transition between stability and instability. Infinitely many minimizers require more refined analysis than finitely many.

The authors also prove that stability of the functions implies stability of the actual cluster centers. This connects the mathematical formulation back to the concrete output of K-means. Because practitioners use stability to select the number of clusters, the authors present the analysis as a starting point for theoretically justified selection rules, rather than a completed rule for choosing K.
neurips-2006-stability-of-k-means-cluste.tldr: K-means stability depends on the geometry and uniqueness of its optimal solutions, with multiple optima producing a square-root sample-change threshold.

paragraphs: A point cloud can contain several geometric structures with different intrinsic dimensions. This paper studies data sampled from a stratification: a collection of manifolds that need not all have the same dimension. It addresses the need to describe such mixed structure, including differences in how densely the individual regions are populated.

The proposed method jointly performs soft clustering and estimates dimensionality and density. Soft clustering allows membership to remain uncertain rather than immediately assigning every observation to one group. The framework uses maximum likelihood estimation for a Poisson mixture model, bringing the grouping of points and the characterization of their underlying structures into one statistical procedure.

Artificial and real examples illustrate why extending manifold learning to stratification learning matters. A description of a point cloud may need to account for both its geometric dimensions and its sampling densities across different components. The contribution is a method that estimates these properties together, treating mixed dimensionality as part of the structure to be learned rather than requiring one shared dimensional description.
neurips-2006-stratification-learning-det.tldr: A Poisson mixture approach jointly estimates soft clusters, densities, and differing intrinsic dimensions in point clouds sampled from multiple manifolds.

paragraphs: Recognizing a motorcycle and distinguishing between motorcycle types are related but different tasks. This paper draws on psychological observations that broad categories are often defined by their parts, while finer categories depend more on the properties of those parts. It uses that distinction to organize recognition into two learning stages.

First, the method learns a relational model of parts from unsegmented images belonging to the broader category. That model converts each image into a category-specific vector whose entries correspond to model parts. Second, a standard discriminative classifier learns to distinguish subclasses using those vectors. The broad category therefore provides the representation used for finer distinctions.

Experiments cover several subclasses. The proposed approach typically performs better than a competing one-stage algorithm and a two-stage method based on a model of the narrower subclass. These results support learning shared part structure at the broader category level before classifying subclasses. The reported advantage is typical across the experiments, rather than a claim that the approach wins in every case.
neurips-2006-subordinate-class-recogniti.tldr: Learning shared object parts at the broad-category level provides a representation that typically improves recognition of finer subclasses.

paragraphs: This paper asks what information about visual stimuli can be read from neural activity over time. The authors use recordings from multiple electrodes in cat primary visual cortex and test whether a simple linear classifier can identify information about the stimuli that were presented.

They find that stimulus information is extractable and remains available for several hundred milliseconds after the stimulus disappears. During rapid sequences of presentations, the recordings contain information about both earlier and newer stimuli at the same time. The neural representation therefore retains information from recent input while also representing what has arrived more recently.

The authors also find that nonlinear relationships between stimuli can be extracted. Together, these observations suggest nonlinear properties in the cortical representations being measured. The significance lies in the combination of persistence and coexistence: information about sequential inputs overlaps in time, and the representation supports information about their relationships. The paper discusses what these findings imply for nonlinear theories of brain computation, grounding that discussion in the recorded visual cortical activity.
neurips-2006-temporal-dynamics-of-inform.tldr: Cat visual cortex recordings retain information about past stimuli alongside new ones and support extraction of nonlinear relationships between them.
